newsitem.title: IRAN: Moderate Iran president taking office, faces tests.
newsitem.headline: Moderate Iran president taking office, faces tests.

text.p: Iran's new President Mohammad Khatami, known for his moderate views, formally takes office on Monday and will turn to choosing his cabinet in a first test of strength with a conservative Islamic parliament.

Khatami takes the oath of office three months after his stunning election victory over a conservative foe and analysts said he will then try to consolidate his power for a possible effort to introduce social and economic reforms.

Khatami, 54, has yet to announce his cabinet list but it is expected to include representatives of various groups which gave him an overwhelming election victory and at the same time seek to appease religious hardliners.

"It will be difficult to balance all these forces but at least the conservative wing accepted his victory and opened the door slightly for a possible easing-up in the (Islamic) system," said one Western diplomat.
Analysts expect the first test of Khatami's future dealings with the conservative-dominated parliament in Tehran to come when he seeks approval for his cabinet.

"They are watching out for any sign he is too liberal, moving too far, too soon, (so that they can) create a symbolic issue to trip him," one analyst said of the parliament led by speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri -- a hardliner who many expected would beat Khatami handily in the presidential election.
Nateq-Nouri was among the conservatives who forced Khatami to resign as culture minister in 1992 for failing to fight what they saw as a Western cultural invasion.
Khatami, seen as a moderate middle-level clergyman in the Iranian context, has not indicated when he would present his cabinet to parliament or disclose the names of main candidates.

One Iranian businessman said Khatami ..."has to be far more clever to succeed in opening up the country and I do not see that in him". The businessman predicted a deadlock with conservatives before the end of the year.
On Sunday, Khatami was confirmed as president by Iran's supreme Shi'ite Moslem patriarch, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who said that he was certain the new president would stay on Iran's "Islamic path".

Scores of foreign ambassadors attended the ceremony but European Union envoys who were invited did not because of an unresolved EU-Iranian dispute. EU envoys were also unlikely to attend Monday's swearing-in at the parliament.

EU states recalled their envoys from Tehran following Iran's implication last May by a German court in the 1992 murder in Berlin of four Iranian Kurds. When they decided to send them back, Iran said the German ambassador should be the last to arrive.
That condition was rejected by the EU.
It proposed working around the demand by making other EU ambassadors fly back to Tehran with the German envoy who would be the last man off the aircraft. Iran rebuffed the proposal.
"The EU will not send back the ambassadors if the German ambassador is the last one in," said one diplomat. "It is self-protection because it could happen to any of us in the future."
Many Iranians who voted for Khatami said they hoped he would resolve foreign policy problems that have caused tensions in Iran's relations with the West and Arab neighbours.

But diplomats said Khatami would commit political suicide if he tried early in his presidency to resolve the dispute over late Iranian leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's death edict against British author Salman Rushdie for his novel "The Satanic Verses", seen by many Moslem states as blasphemous.

Also, pursuing any immediate effort to re-establish direct contacts with Washington, broken after the Khomeini-led 1979 revolution that toppled Iran's U.S.-backed monarchy, could endanger his domestic position, one diplomat said.

"He has first to consolidate his power and achieve some progress on the economic front," he said. "Even if there is some public support to improve Iran's international image, the (troubled) economy is his first priority.
"(Khatami) was elected because of economic and social pressures and he must be seen as responding to the demands of the 20 million people who voted for him."
